etymology.root: wing + tip, a plain compound; the piece also answers to flapper and to pointer, and all three names describe the same shape from a different angle
etymology.note: Wikipedia's Buffalo wing article names the three segments "drumette, flat, and flapper or pointer"; its poultry article gives "the wing tip (also called the 'flapper')". *Inference —* tip is what a butcher calls it, flapper what a cook calls it, pointer what a diner calls it when handed one.

text.what: Third segment, the pointed end. Skin, cartilage, two slivers of bone, almost no meat. Usually cut off before the wing reaches a fryer and boiled into stock instead, though some restaurants serve it still joined to the flat.
text.how: Where it survives on the plate, it is eaten whole — crust, cartilage and all — or left in the bone bowl. Where it does not, it goes into a stockpot: collagen from the joints is what makes chicken stock set, so the least saleable piece of the wing is the one worth most to a kitchen that makes its own.
